title: Sources of genetic variation in meiosis and fertilization; Monohybrid inheritance and Punnett squares
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: IN01#t2 term and clue written for the game; IN01#t1 term and clue written for the game; CD04#t3 term and clue written for the game; CD04#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD04#N.6, IN01#N.3, CD04#N.12b, IN01#N.8b, CD04#N.13, IN01#N.10, IN01#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Locus
items.clue: Position of a gene on a chromosome.

items.label: Allele
items.clue: One of the different forms of the same gene.

items.label: Bivalent
items.clue: A pair of homologues joined together in prophase I

items.label: Chiasmata
items.clue: The points where non-sister chromatids break and rejoin

questions.stem: Which statement describes crossing over during meiosis?

options.text: The two sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange their segments in prophase I.
At a chiasma, all four chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments in prophase I.
Non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments in prophase I.
Homologous pairs swap the sides of the plate they face at metaphase I.

questions.explanation: While homologues are paired in prophase I, non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding segments at chiasmata, making new combinations of alleles.

questions.stem: In peas the allele T for tall stems is dominant to the allele t for dwarf stems, and TT and Tt plants are equally tall. What is the reason that the heterozygote is not shorter than the homozygous dominant plant?

options.text: The T allele switches off the t allele in the heterozygote, so the plant effectively has two working T alleles
Tall plants are more common than dwarf plants, so the tall allele is the stronger one and takes over
One T allele makes enough functional protein for full stem growth, so the t allele has no observable effect
The heterozygote is in fact slightly shorter, because a single T allele makes half as much of the protein as two

questions.stem: In a hypothetical animal with 2n = 10, nondisjunction produces an egg with 6 chromosomes. The egg is fertilized by a normal sperm, and the zygote develops into an offspring. Which prediction about the offspring's body cells is correct?

options.text: Only its reproductive cells would have 11 chromosomes; the rest would have 10.
Every body cell would have 10 chromosomes, because fertilization restores the diploid number.
Its cells would have 10 or 11, since mitosis gives daughter cells different chromosomes.
Every body cell would have 11 chromosomes, copied from the zygote by mitosis.

questions.explanation: The zygote has 6 + 5 = 11 chromosomes. Mitosis gives every daughter cell the same chromosomes, so every body cell has 11.

questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele of an autosomal gene. Two parents who are both heterozygous for this gene have three children, all of whom have cystic fibrosis. Which statement correctly describes the probability that their fourth child will have cystic fibrosis?

options.text: It is 1/4, because each child's genotype is independent of the others'.
It is 1/256, because four affected children in a row would be very unlikely.
It is 1, because all three of the couple's earlier children have been affected.
It is 1/2, because the child will either have cystic fibrosis or not have it.

questions.explanation: Each child receives c from each heterozygous parent with probability 1/2, so P(cc) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The three earlier children do not change this probability.

questions.stem: A mutation in a hypothetical species of animal prevents crossing over during meiosis, but meiosis is otherwise normal. Compared with the gametes of a normal individual, which prediction about the gametes of an individual with this mutation is correct?

options.text: Every gamete would be genetically identical, since crossing over is the only source of genetic variation.
They would vary less but still differ, because homologous pairs still orient randomly at metaphase I.
They would vary just as much as before, since crossing over just swaps sister chromatid segments.
Each gamete would carry either the full maternal or the full paternal set of chromosomes.

questions.stem: To find out whether a purple-flowered pea plant is homozygous (PP) or heterozygous (Pp), a breeder crosses it with a white-flowered plant (pp). Why is a white-flowered plant used for this test cross?

options.text: Its white colour dilutes the purple, so the shade of the offspring shows the purple plant's genotype.
It passes on only p, so each offspring's colour shows the allele it received from the purple plant.
It has no allele for flower colour, so the offspring carry the purple plant's alleles alone.
It passes on both of its p alleles, so every offspring is white unless it also receives P.

questions.stem: In mice, the allele B for black fur is dominant to the allele b for brown fur. A black mouse of unknown genotype is crossed with a brown mouse. Of the 9 offspring, 5 are black and 4 are brown. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The black mouse is BB, because a mouse that shows the dominant trait must be homozygous.
The genotype cannot be decided, because 5 : 4 is not exactly the 1 : 1 expected from a test cross.
The black mouse is Bb, because each brown offspring must have received b from it.
The black mouse is BB, and the brown offspring arose from new mutations in its gametes.
